name: Alexis de Tocqueville
role: French political thinker and historian, deputy (1839-1851) and foreign minister (1849)
summary: Tocqueville accepted the spread of equality as an irreversible, providential development and sought to protect liberty within it, through local self-government, juries, independent courts, free associations and a free press, against the tyranny of the majority and centralized administration. He defended property and opposed socialism and a state-guaranteed right to work, held religion necessary to free democracies while keeping clergy out of politics, and backed French conquest and settlement of Algeria while accepting harsh wartime methods.

separated-powers.rationale: In the Recollections he describes arguing in the 1848 constitutional committee for the system of counterpoises against a single chamber, and Democracy in America presents the federal form, municipal institutions and an independent judiciary as the barriers that restrain majority despotism.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: He calls the American courts' power to declare statutes unconstitutional one of the most powerful barriers ever devised against the tyranny of political assemblies, and says judges check the majority without stopping its activity.

second-chamber.rationale: On the 1848 constitutional committee he opposed the single-chamber proposal and sided with the dual-chamber minority, which he says was defeated with only three votes on his side.

indirect-election.rationale: In the 1848 committee he proposed that the President be chosen by delegates elected by the people, with the Assembly choosing if no absolute majority emerged, an idea he says he took from the American Constitution; the first part was rejected.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: He moved in committee that the President not be elected directly by the citizens (lost), though he later accepted that once direct election was decided it would be rash to restrict the people's choice.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Democracy in America argues that a re-eligible president becomes an easy tool of the majority, and in 1848 he vigorously backed barring re-election, but he later called that vote a mistake once the President was to be elected directly, so the position is mixed.

term-limits.rationale: He backed a no-re-election rule for the presidency in 1848 and argued against re-eligibility in Democracy in America, but regretted the vote in light of direct election, and he says nothing about legislators or other offices.

constitutional-jury-trial.rationale: He devotes a chapter to the jury as an eminently republican political institution, in civil as well as criminal cases, and says he is convinced of its value; he does not discuss a constitutional guarantee as such.

decide-locally.rationale: He praises American municipal freedom and the absence of centralized administration as the training ground of liberty, and warns that centralized administration accustoms men to set their will aside, while still accepting a strong central government for general interests.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Democracy in America presents township meetings, juries and local office-holding as the schools in which citizens learn self-government, though he does not argue for workplace or university democracy.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: He argues that democratic nations need associations more than any, as the only permanent protection against the despotism of faction or a single individual, which is the opposite of bypassing intermediate groups.

suppress-opposition.rationale: He holds that the right of association and the independent press are the guarantees of liberty against majority and princely despotism, and in conversation condemns Louis Napoleon's suppression of the press and tribune.

party-controls-media.rationale: He writes that censorship of the press and universal suffrage are irreconcilable and that the press is the only guarantee of citizens' liberty and security; he approves it more from the evils it prevents than from enthusiasm for it.

job-guarantee.rationale: In the Constituent Assembly on 12 September 1848 he spoke against writing a right to work into the constitution, warning that guaranteeing work would make the state the organizer of labor, and the amendment failed 396 to 187.

property-fundamental.rationale: In his January 1848 Chamber speech he treats property as the last remaining right under assault from democratic opinion, and in the 1848 Assembly he defended individual property against socialist doctrines; he does not state it as an absolute.

central-planning.rationale: In the right-to-work speech he rejects making the state the great and only organizer of labor as the road to servitude, and says democracy and socialism are contrary.

public-ownership.rationale: He says nothing authorizes the state to step into the middle of industry and that it would be drawn into becoming an industrialist, which he opposes.

state-directs-investment.rationale: He objects that a state guaranteeing work would be drawn into becoming the industrialist and would use taxation as the main means of feeding industry, and he rejects that role for the state.

land-redistribution.rationale: He opposes the doctrines that deny the rights of property and praises the Revolution for having peopled France with ten million proprietors, rejecting taking property from owners.

night-watchman-state.rationale: In the same speech he backs public assistance to those who suffer as Christian charity applied to politics, so he does not limit government to defence, justice and property, though he opposes state direction of industry.

cut-welfare.rationale: He supports public aid to those in need while refusing to make it a constitutional right to work or to put state foresight in the place of individual foresight.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: He calls the manufacturing aristocracy among the harshest ever, if confined and least dangerous, and says that if permanent inequality returns it will enter by that channel, so democracy's friends should watch it.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: He warns that the taste for physical gratification can shut out the rest of the world and come between the soul and heaven, but he also says it is a confined passion that leads democratic peoples into no great excesses.

separate-church-state.rationale: He holds that state religions always become fatal to the Church, that clergy taking part in public affairs endangers belief, and says he would rather shut the priesthood within the sanctuary; he finds American religion strongest because separated from the state.

reason-over-faith.rationale: He argues that dogmatical belief, taken on trust, is indispensable to individuals and to society, and that religious dogma is the most desirable kind, so reason alone cannot be the only guide.

spiritual-nature.rationale: He argues that belief in the immortality of the soul is the great benefit of religion for democracies, and that governments should act as if they believed in it and conform to religious morality in great affairs.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: He says Christianity must be maintained at any cost in modern democracies and that despotism may govern without faith but liberty cannot, which is the opposite of state-promoted atheism.

national-church-status.rationale: He states that he has always held that state religions, though sometimes of momentary service to political power, always become fatal to the Church.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: He approves the American practice of two distinct lines of action for the sexes, saying they have excellently understood democratic improvement while keeping woman's social inferiority, though he describes custom more than law.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: He reports without objection that Americans hold man to be the natural head of the conjugal association and says democracy's object is to regulate power, not subvert it, praising their approach.

hereditarian-race.rationale: In his 1853 letter to Gobineau he says the doctrine that races have insuperable capacities is probably quite false and certainly very pernicious, and that it has never been proved.

remove-indigenous-peoples.rationale: Democracy in America condemns the removal of the Cherokees, Choctaws and Creeks as a legalized destruction, remarking sarcastically that it is impossible to destroy men with more respect for the laws of humanity.

treaties-binding.rationale: He criticizes the federal government for making treaties with the Indians as independent nations and then abandoning them to the legislative tyranny of the states, reporting the Cherokees' complaint without qualification.

restore-past-order.rationale: The introduction calls the gradual development of equality a providential fact that cannot be checked by one generation and sets the author's task as guiding democracy, not restoring the old order.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: He says he knows no country with so little true independence of mind and freedom of discussion as America because the majority controls the will, though he does not call for encouraging eccentric lives.

traditional-family.rationale: He writes that no free community ever existed without morals and that morals are the work of woman, and praises the strict marriage morals of America as a source of its strength, without defending any particular family form in law.

premarital-sex.rationale: He praises the strict sexual morals of America, where books suppose women chaste, while condemning the double standard that excuses the seducer, so he does not treat sex outside marriage as acceptable.

conscription.rationale: In a letter to Senior during the Crimean War he says he does not see how Britain can hold its rank unless its people consent to something resembling a conscription.

war-builds-character.rationale: He writes that he speaks no ill of war, which almost always enlarges the mind of a people and raises their character, and can check the excesses that grow from equality, while warning that it cannot cure the army's ambition.

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: In his 1841 Algeria report he calls burning harvests, emptying silos and seizing unarmed men, women and children regrettable necessities that anyone making war on the Arabs must accept, and says the right of war allows ravaging the country.

non-intervention.rationale: As foreign minister in 1849 he instructed that the treaties gave France no right to intervene in the Hungarian war, but he also directed and defended the French intervention at Rome, so his record points both ways.

notes: Mature positions are taken from Democracy in America (1835-40), his 1848-49 political record and later conversation. The 1851 resistance to the coup, the 1840s report on Algerian colonization and his Memoir on Pauperism were not found in an open full text and are not used. Opinions on universal suffrage and aristocracy in conversation with Senior were qualified by Tocqueville himself in footnotes, so they are left null. Themes searched: economy, government (executive, chambers, courts, local government, press, association), society and religion, race and slavery, women, war and empire, foreign policy in 1849. No position was found on immigration, trade, environment, technology or most identity-politics statements.
